subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY

speechtext: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister) moved the third reading of Bill No. 21, to amend the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: TRANSFER TO PARLIAMENT OF CONTROL OF EXPORT EXCEPT IN INTERNATIONAL EMERGENCY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, few measures better illustrate the value of parliamentary discussion than the one now before us for third reading. We have, I believe in a not unfriendly spirit, discussed the proposals submitted by the government, and I think the adoption of suggestions by the government in the form of amendments has improved greatly the legislation. Yet I feel it would be most unfair, not only to myself but to many others who are associated with me, if I did not indicate that it is a little difficult even yet to understand how a private act of parliament should determine an issue so fully national and so very important in the largest and truest sense as that concerning the exportation of power.
I have only this further observation to make. While the executive may or may not be the best body to determine whether licences for the export of power should be issued, there can be no doubt about one thing, that they are as competent to determine that matter as they are to determine whether a statute of this parliament should be repealed. Inasmuch as the executive is now being vested with the power to repeal a statute, which repeal would from necessity arise from knowledge possessed by the executive as to the wisdom or unwisdom of the continuance of the statute, it should follow that the same executive is quite capable of fulfilling the obligation placed upon it by the original statute, namely, of determining whether or not licences should issue. If the power to repeal the statute is not as great as the

Inspection and Sale Act
power to determine whether licences should issue, it is hard to understand what is the true measure of responsibility.
That is all I have to say. I do not intend either to discuss anew the merits or demerits of the measure, or to move an amendment to refer it back to the committee. I content myself with saying that for the reasons indicated I shall have to say "nay" to the motion for third reading.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada

the same spirit as that which has inspired my right hon. friend, I desire to thank him and the hon. members on his side for their suggestions, some of which have been embodied in the bill. subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES

speechtext:
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize the guarantee by the government of Canada of principal and interest of loans made by chartered banks and guaranteed by the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, respectively, for the purchase of seed grain and for providing other assistance to farmers in connection with seeding operations during the spring of 1938; the liability of the government of Canada in respect of such guarantees not to exceed in the aggregate the sum of $1,900,000 in respect of Alberta and $14,500,000 in respect of Saskatchewan.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the bill to be based on this resolution represents the national aspect of an effort to ensure that those portions of the prairie provinces which

Seed Grain

were ravaged by drought in 1937 will once more be sown. The principle of the measure is identical with that of the one passed at the last session of parliament under which guarantees were given for the seeding operations of 1937.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Yes, I will a little later.
The amounts involved differ because of the different area affected as compared with the area in 1936. In 1937 severe drought conditions affected Manitoba less than previously, with the result that Manitoba is not this year included within the bill to be based upon this resolution. In Saskatchewan the intensity and area affected was greater than ever before, and the problem consequently in that province is much more serious. The government of Alberta asks for a somewhat larger provision than a year ago, but not materially so. Last year the limit of our guarantee in the case of Alberta was $1,600,000. By the resolution now under consideration for this year the amount is $1,900,000. In the case of Saskatchewan last year the limit of our guarantee was $6,600,000, and this year the amount asked for in that province is $14,500,000.
I have spoken of the much wider area affected this year. Another factor which affects the figures is the higher prices which must be paid for seed grain, feed grain and fodder for use during the seeding period. In asking us to guarantee loans up to $1,900,000, the province of Alberta states that the number of farmers applying for assistance in this respect will be about 15.000. The amount required in this area in Alberta will be about $1,800,000, while the further sum of $100,000 will be required in that province to provide similar assistance in what may be called marginal districts.
The actual loans made in Alberta last year totalled $1,339,328; that is to say, the amount authorized by this parliament in respect of that province was not fully required. As at December 31, 1937, reflecting the somewhat better crop conditions in some parts of Alberta and as a result of repayments made out of last year's crop, the amount outstanding under the Alberta guarantee for last year has been reduced to $919,000.
In the case of Saskatchewan the number of farmer applicants has greatly increased because of the condition I mentioned a few moments ago. The government of that province estimates that the number of farmers who will need some kind of seeding assistance

because of the lack of production last year will exceed 81,000, as compared with 25,000 who received assistance last year. These are just round figures.
The amounts required for the various forms of assistance in each province have been carefully considered by the federal Department of Agriculture together with representatives of the department of agriculture in each of the provinces concerned, and my colleague the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will be able to answer all questions with respect to thr provincial method of determining how seed shall be supplied in detail and the terms upon which it is made available to the individual farmer.
Subject to further questions-of course the members of the committee are free to ask questions, and I have here all the information with respect to the whole history of seed grain advances during the last seven or eight unfortunate years-I would say that this represents what appears to this government and to the governments of the two provinces concerned as the most effective means of ensuring that this great area shall be sown this coming spring.
I said a year ago in discussing this matter that all Canada had recognized and appreciated the fact that the drought problem had assumed the proportions of a national emergency, and it is in that spirit that all those concerned approach the problem we have before us this afternoon. This measure represents cooperation, starting with the individual farmer, his municipality, his province, the federal government, and the chartered banks. The amounts here represented by the guarantee figures do not represent all of the advances which will be made by the chartered banks. For instance, in the case of Saskatchewan it is estimated that the advances by the banks will run to over $18,000,000 for these purposes. The mortgage companies, having the interest of a mortgagee in lands, are by provincial legislation enabled to advance seed grain to their mortgagors, arid it is anticipated that they will do so to the extent of between $1,000,000 and $1,250,000. I think therefore it can be said that this measure does represent definite cooperation between all those interested to give another chance, and a chance I think under better moisture conditions than have been apparent at this time of year in that area for a number of years past, to the people in this great area to produce a crop once more. 1 am positive in stating that without a measure of this kind it would be quite impossible for millions of acres of our most fertile land to be sown to wheat this spring.

speechtext:
An article appeared in the Alberta papers on March 15 from which I quote:
Expenditure of $1,900,000 by the federal government on seed and seeding operations in Alberta this year was announced Monday by Hon. J. G. Gardiner, federal minister of agriculture, after a conference with Hon. D. B. Mullen, Alberta minister of agriculture.
According to the press report the minister was going to have the federal government spend $1,900,000 in the province of Alberta-before the election, an hon. member suggests.
Mr. Gardiner said the resolution on which the legislation will be based providing for the $1,900,000 for seed and seeding operations in Alberta was now before parliament.
After reading such reports in the press, I am not surprised that the cabinet of a Liberal government should disallow legislation designed to give the citizens of Alberta accurate news and information.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
As the minister has stated, this is a very important measure, the purpose of which is to provide seed for a very large area in the province of Saskatchewan; and it will affect very much the returns that the farmers of that province will have next fall. That means also that it will affect the whole business of this dominion. It is important because, as has been stated, it provides for the distribution of seed, of feed for horses, and of power, by means of gasoline and repairs, for seeding the crop.
I regret however that the minister did not see fit to bring in thfe measure earlier. When one considers the importance of it, the present date, March 25, is quite late to introduce it. It is only right to expect that the minister will find it necessary to give details with respect to the whole question of conditions in western Canada. He has already mentioned the number of farmers that are affected this year, namely 81,000, but we shall also require details with respect to the area involved and the accumulation and distribution of the seed. However the proper time to obtain such details will be when the bill is in committee.
May I remind the committee that on a former occasion, in 1933, when Saskatchewan and other western provinces needed seed for their spring requirements-the area not quite
Seed Grain

so large as the present one, but being very considerable-a measure for the distribution of seed was introduced as early as February 1.
I might add that it was held up for nearly two months; in fact on April 1 the government of the day had to employ the closure to get the measure through. Under all the circumstances I believe members of the government and all other hon. members will agree that we shall be acting in a kindly spirit if we facilitate the passing of this measure in good time, without regard to the delay caused five years ago by the details that were demanded and * the questions that were asked. I do not think our present course will be calculated to delay this measure in any particular, although it is quite evident that we might do so if we so desired.
I am informed on pretty good authority that a request was made about January 29 by the government of Saskatchewan to the federal government for about S27,000,000 to provide seed and fodder for spring requirements. I will not go into details as to how this amount was made up, but the minister might let us know whether such a requisition was made by the provincial government on or about that time. If it was, it should not have taken the government all this time to decide what they would do about it; they should have known long before this. The minister might also inform us if the Minister of Agriculture held a meeting with the loan companies and the banks early in February, either here or in Toronto, when the whole question was discussed, including the provincial government's requisition.
I shall not argue the point as to whether $14,500,000 is sufficient. I believe it is. Of course price must be considered, but if proper distribution is made and the situation is efficiently handled this sum may be sufficient. The one point about which I am distressed is this. In the four years prior to 1935 relief and seed distribution was handled in Saskatchewan by a commission. It did a good job, and there was no criticism, at least not to be compared with what we hear to-day on all sides with respect to the quantity of seed to be provided and the number of acres to be seeded. The commission had its inspectors in the different municipalities; requisition was made to them and considered by the inspector concerned, and the farmer got his seed on reasonable conditions. But the regulations that have been issued by the provincial government which is now in power are such as easily lend themselves to some degree of discrimination and political favouritism. I referred a minute ago to the fact that we have

not criticized this government very much. I believe we have been kind to them as regards the distribution of relief in Saskatchewan, not merely with regard to seed, but other matters as well. We have received plenty of information which leads us to believe that the handling of relief in Saskatchewan since 1934 has been a scandal and a disgrace, and I believe that if a committee were set up to investigate, we could prove it. There has been a lack of control of prices, and many other things could be brought up. However, this perhaps is not the time to enter into a discussion of that matter.
Will the minister also inform us whether any requests have been made by the provincial government that they be permitted to finance or assist municipalities in providing tractor power for seeding this spring, owing to the fact that there has been very great mortality among the horses of the province and there is a deplorable situation from the standpoint of horse power this spring? Reports have been coming forward regarding the loss of horses and in many municipalities it is over fifty per cent-that is, horses that died in the municipality during the winter, and the loss of horses shipped to the feeding ground in Manitoba, many of which have not returned. Many of the horses that are being returned to the province from the feeding ground in Manitoba are in a weakened condition and I was wondering whether any requisition had been made to the government for assistance to the farmers in the form of tractors for their seeding. When we get into committee on the bill I shall ask for more details with respect to many of these matters, particularly the purchasing of seed and the question of the premiums that were paid. I think we shall have to ascertain how they arrived at the price of $1.45 to the farmers.
At the present time the soil and moisture condition in the province is very favourable and the prospects for a crop are fairly good. In the last seven or eight years we have not had such favourable soil and moisture conditions for the reception of seed. The Minister of Agriculture has just returned from the province and he may be able to enlighten us in that regard. That being the situation, it is important that every possible acre that is suitable should be seeded this year. Many districts have not had a crop in five or six years and it would be serious and most regrettable if every possible acre were not seeded this year so as to give the farmers a break. I have received hundreds of letters protesting

Seed Grain
and expressing dissatisfaction with the regulations that have been issued by the provincial government with respect to the amount of seed which will be provided for the individual farmer. A report in the Regina Daily Star of March 22 is to the effect that the Liberal members of the provincial legislature are themselves concerned. The report is headed:
Hear Liberals Trying for More Seed Wheat.
Possibly it is just a hitch in banking arrangements, a ripple in administration that will shortly be ironed out, but some private members of the legislature insist there is now being carried on extensive negotiations with Ottawa in an effort to secure more seed and easier terms. It is further rumoured that important news is expected shortly from men who have something to do with the federal treasury.
The report goes on to state that a special session may be called. This is from Liberal members of the Saskatchewan legislature.
If Ottawa "fails to come through" in the next few hours, the members may be called back to Regina within a week for a short and special session to deal with one matter only-more seed grain and particularly more seed wheat.

I would advise hon. members to read also the Free Press and the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix; if they do they will get some interesting information. This report states that a whole trainload of horses had to be unloaded at Areola before they got to their various destinations. Some had to be taken out and a veterinary called; then they were reloaded and taken to various places, such as Creelman and Fillmore. Some had to be taken to farms on stone-boats. That is a serious matter and it explains why there is a shortage of horse power in the province. In my opinion the farmers in certain parts of that province would be justified in asking the government to give them some compensation for the loss they have suffered in horses, particularly those shipped to the feeding ground in Manitoba. They were encouraged to ship the horses, in fact they were forced to do so because feed was not provided in Saskatchewan, and when the horses were shipped out they should have been properly cared for. As I have said, however, many of the horses are returning in a terribly weakened condition and they will not be able to cope with the spring work. That is why I suggest that the government should assist the farmers in providing tractors to put in the crop, because fifty per cent of the horses will not be able to go into spring work at all. speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Chairman. As the Minister of Finance has just said, this matter has been under discussion for the last six months. In the first place it is necessary to secure sufficient quantities of the different types of grain to be used for seeding purposes. That is the first job to be done. In the second place it is necessary to invite everyone who has a real interest in the matter to see that seed is provided. As has been suggested by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle, some weeks ago I did interview the loan company representatives in Toronto, and discussed with them the extent to which they would be able to assist in putting sufficient capital at the disposal of someone so that seed would be put in on the land in which they have an interest. 1 must say that we have always found the loan companies, whether in eastern or western Canada, quite ready to do everything they possibly can to cooperate with governments in putting seed in any of the lands on which they have made loans, and this year has been no exception. As the Minister of Finance has said, as the result of those discussions the loan companies are providing somewhere between a million and a million and a quarter dollars for the purpose of putting seed upon lands in certain sections of the west in which they have an interest.
There were discussions also with the -banks as to the extent to which they could assist in providing finances for the purpose of furnishing seed to farmers. There were also discussions with the municipal authorities-not the municipalities as such, but officials who have to do with the central organizations of municipal bodies-and there were discussions with the provincial governments. On a number of occasions I have interviewed members of the governments of both Alberta and Saskatchewan and we discussed the question very fully with them. It is always true that when you begin to talk in the first instance you start out with a much larger sum of money in mind than the amount finally arrived at as actually necessary to provide what is needed. But I must say that in both Saskatchewan and Alberta agreement was reached between this government and the two provincial governments as to the amount of guarantee required in each province.
Seed Grain

The Minister of Finance has already-explained that the amount of $14,500,000 for Saskatchewan is not the total that will be provided by the banks in order to finance seeding operations in that province. My understanding is that the $1,900,000 provided for Alberta will be the total, and this amount will be guaranteed in connection with that province. For the benefit of the hon. member from Alberta who spoke a few moments ago, while I am not in the habit of saying that newspaper reports are wrong, still the statement I gave in Alberta, which probably was misunderstood by some, was exactly the statement that has just been made by the Minister of Finance-that this was a guarantee; that the money required would be supplied by the banks to the municipalities, which in turn would supply seed to farmers whose applications were passed upon by the municipal organizations.
The other question raised, with regard to provision for live stock or for power in order to put in the crop, is not an immediate concern of this government. It is the concern of the provincial governments. The $14,500,000 guarantee for Saskatchewan, to be furnished the municipalities by the banks, is presumed to make available sufficient money to take care of all the activities the provincial government think it wise to pursue in order to assist in putting in the crop. As to the method that will be followed; as to whether it will be the encouragement of the old habit among the farmers-I think it is the habit in Saskatchewan as well as elsewhere-to cooperate as far as possible in making use of any power available in the community, whether it be tractor power or horse power, in order to put in the crop in that community; or whether it be by the method of providing fuel to some for tractor power and feed and fodder to others for horse power, I feel quite satisfied that the government in each province, in cooperation with the municipalities, will make what arrangements are necessary in order to see that the crop is put in. I believe, too, that the greater part of that cooperation will be among the farmers in different communities. The general practice has been that where a man has no horses, as a result of his horses having died, the government does give some assistance through this guarantee. That is, the man may be enabled to hire a tractor, perhaps, that is owned by some neighbour, and that is not in use. The tractor may be even in a village. The tractor is hired and the fuel is provided in order that the crop may be put into the ground. But all these activities are carried on by the provincial government

in cooperation with the municipal councils, and I think that is the proper place to leave them.
The question whether or not horses have come back in poor shape is not one with which I can deal, other than to say that in all the checks I have been able to make- and I have been over quite a part of the area during the last few weeks-I have not found that great numbers of horses have died; I have not found that they are any poorer than they usually are after going through a year of this kind, in any part of the dominion. It is perfectly true that if you put a number of horses, cattle, or any other live stock into a box car and carry them three or four hundred miles probably you will have to take one of them home on a stone-boat, as the result of what they do to one another during the journey. You may even have to take one out that is not worth hauling home, but these stories are very much enlarged upon, and the checks we have been able to make indicate that the death rate among live stock this year is not materially greater than in any average year in western Canada.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
The minister mentioned the difficulty of getting seed together. After all this is not a measure to provide seed; it is merely to guarantee amounts of money. The question of the seed hardly impinges upon the computing of the amount of money the government would have to guarantee. However, there is no use labouring the point. I do not say that any harm has been done anyone, but I do say that the lateness of the date makes necessary haste in passing this resolution, which makes it impossible, perhaps, to secure information one would like to have if one had more time in which to ask questions and to deliberate as one ought upon this legislation. I do not feel satisfied as yet in regard to the statement the minister has made, but I have no doubt he will want to enlarge upon it when the bill itself comes down. I should like to know what acreage will be affected and whether the Minister of Finance thinks this amount will be sufficient to meet the situation. For instance, I notice that the number of farmers in Saskatchewan who applied last year was 25,000, while this year the number is 81,000. Assuming that they will need the same amount of seed, that means that more than three times what was supplied last year will have to be supplied this year, whereas the bill provides for only a little over twice as much. On the suggested basis of 250 acres for 81,000 farmers, the total

Seed Grain
would be 20,125,000 acres. At the price suggested, this would mean a figure between $28,000,000 and $30,000,000. I should like the minister to give us some idea as to whether the amounts we are guaranteeing will be sufficient to enable the farmers to put in a reasonable crop.
I think we are all agreed that moisture conditions in western Canada are better to-day than they have been for the past seven or eight years. Prices have improved, and with conditions in Europe what they are, they may be even better in the near future. It would be a tragedy if at this time the crops in Saskatchewan and Alberta were seriously curtailed because sufficient seed was not available to the farmers. I think we should have some information in connection with the suggestion of the minister of agriculture of Saskatchewan as to the maximum acreage for each farmer being 250. We ought to know whether that suggestion is acceptable to the federal government. Personally I think some other basis should be used. In and around the Regina plains, down through Yellow Grass, Riceton and Rouleau, you will find many farmers farming anywhere from one to five sections of land. If such a farmer has no seed available it may mean that he can put in only 250 acres. The result would be that a large part of his farm would be left to go into weeds. The farmer might not have the necessary fuel to operate his tractors-these farmers are all tractor farmers-in order to keep the weeds down and a serious situation might develop.
I suggest some other basis be used. I do not mean that these people should be given all the seed they want, but it could be worked out on a pro rata basis. A man with 200 acres would receive a certain amount, a man with from 200 to 500 acres would receive a certain percentage, and a man having over 500 acres would receive a percentage. Before the bill is brought down we ought to have some information as to the price to !be charged. It has been suggested in Saskatchewan that the farmer will be charged between $1.40 and $1.45 per bushel. That is an exorbitant price and we ought to know just what will be charged. In view of the fact that this government is being asked to guarantee the money, we should have a clear statement as to how a man should go about applying for this seed and upon what basis his application will be accepted or rejected. We should know whether exceptions are to be made to the general regulations. When a man has 'been given a certain amount of seed by the municipal council
we should know whether he can go to the inspector or to someone else and get that amount increased.
We should have particulars of the machinery that is being set up for the distribution of this seed. I think it would be well if the Minister of Agriculture had a copy of the regulations before him when the bill is brought down. Anyone reading the Regina and Saskatoon papers cannot help but be confused by the various suggestions and reports in connection with the regulations to govern the distribution of seed. A clear statement along these lines would help to clarify the whole situation, and I hope the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Agriculture will see fit to give us this information when the 'bill is in committee.

subtopic: GUARANTEE OF LOANS FOR PURCHASE OF SEED AND OTHER ASSISTANCE IN SEEDING OPERATIONS IN WESTERN PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it does appear to me that if this government is to give a guarantee we should know under what conditions we are giving that guarantee. The amounts indicated are $1,900,000 in respect of Alberta, and $14,500,000 in respect of Saskatchewan. Since we are providing the credit by which this money is being obtained from the banks, is it not desirable that full information be given? If it were not for the conditions to which the minister has alluded, it would not be necessary for us to pledge our credit. As the minister has properly remarked to the hon. member for Prince (Mr. MacLean) this is a matter between the provincial governments and the people of the provinces. If the credit of the provincial governments were good, we would not come into the picture at all. It is only because we in the west are unable to deal with the situation that we have to rely upon the credit of the federal government.
Has the seed grain already been provided? Was it secured last fall through the operations of the wheat board? Under what authority does the wheat board function? Was it permitted to buy only from producers? How has this wheat been held? At what price was it acquired? All these are relevant questions that should be dealt with. It seems to me that the government when in opposition would never have permitted a measure such as this to pass unless such information was forthcoming. I do not think the request is an unreasonable one. I have inspected the papers downstairs and I know what provision has been made to acquire this seed. I want to know what price has been paid for the seed grain and what price is to be paid by the farmer. There will be no great freight
Seed Grain

charges to pay on this grain, because it has been taken over in the interior elevators, according to the returns made a week or so ago by the auditors of the wheat board. I think all this information should be in our .possession.
Then you come to the far more difficult question, a question that in days gone by used to be dealt with in a very, shall I say, detailed manner. Some of those who have participated in this debate will perhaps recall their anxiety to know, first, how many acres a man was to be permitted to seed; whether he should have a percentage of his available acreage seeded to -wheat, to oats, to rye and barley; or should it be fixed definitely that no man could seed more than a blank number of acres? To act on such a suggestion would be utterly unfair. A man with a thousand acres would be in a position to have cultivated only the same number of acres as the man with only the minimum number. Attention has been directed to this by the hon. member for Weyburn.
Then you come to the next question, the distribution of the seed grain. There you have a question which unfortunately gets into the realm of politics. When the legislation is before us in committee I propose to suggest that there shall be no departure from the regulations, which I would like to see as a schedule to the bill. I know, as other members know, human nature being what it is, to quote the language of the Prime Minister that you have to consider the pressure that will be brought to bear upon those who are responsible for administration. That pressure takes many forms. You have the municipality and you have the provincial government. The regulations are initiated by the provincial government and are supposed to be made effective by the municipality.
Then there are the inspectors. You have one man with 1.200 acres urging that owing to the splendid moisture content of the soil and the apparent certainty of a crop, an exception should be made in his case and a larger quantity of land made available for cropping than in the case of someone who in his opinion is less fortunately situated. Surely we should try to deal with that so as not to make it possible in this democracy that men may think that their ability to secure a crop depends upon their attitude towards public questions-in other words, depends upon their political faith. It seems to me we must do everything in our power to see that that is not the case. I know something of the difficulties. I did not listen to all the criticisms urged in days gone by without

realizing that this is not a condition applicable only to one individual or set of individuals, but is the common attribute of poor, weak humanity, and that if an election is in sight and the pressure is strong the result is fairly certain. We must do something to prevent that condition arising.
These are the questions upon which we should have information. We start with what has been done with respect to seed and what is involved with respect to cost. Then we come down to our acceptance, mark you, Mr. Chairman, of the regulations promulgated by the province; for the minute we give our guarantee we tacitly admit that the conditions are acceptable to us. We have, therefore a responsibility which I hope we shall exercise not in any narrow spirit but with an earnest desire, as the Minister of Finance has said, to make some little contribution to the national welfare by the creation in this year of grace of a substantial quantity of new wealth-for that is what it means. One of the reasons why a wheat crop is regarded as so valuable is that you sow it in the spring and have new wealth in the fall. It is not like cattle, where the new wealth does not become available for years, or like many other enterprises, in the mining field, for example, where the losses are colossal and now and then you have a great success. But with wheat, if we have a crop at all, we know it will result in a very great expansion of new wealth, and that wealth becomes available in the autumn of the very year in which the crop has been sown. That is why I suggest that the minister should place the information on Hansard, in order that the people may realize the magnitude of the efforts that are being made and the reason why the public credit is being pledged, that of the dominion in addition to the provinces; because according to the terms of the resolution the provinces are giving their undertaking and the municipalities are giving theirs, and the banks are protecting their depositors -on a ten to one basis, I take it?-by the guarantee of the federal government.

In answer to the question asked by the hon. member for Weybum and enlarged upon by the leader of the opposition, I may say that in Saskatchewan they have a Seed Grain Loans Guarantee Act of 1938, which was put through in the recent session. The procedure under that act is this. First the municipality passes a by-law which will enable it to borrow money for seed grain purposes. A copy of the by-law is submitted to the minister of municipal affairs for approval. After approval has been given the municipality approaches the bank and arranges for a loan, giving as security for repayment its demand promissory note bearing interest at the rate of four per cent. Second, the municipality takes from the recipient his demand promissory note as well as a written agreement for a lien upon all crops to be grown during the year in which the note is
Seed Grain

given and the succeeding year on the land named in his application. Third, the rate of interest to be charged farmers by the municipalities is not stipulated in the Saskatchewan Seed Grain and Supply Act. My understanding is that if there is any increase added it will be just sufficient to pay the cost of administration, and that the final rate when payment is made will be four per cent.

municipality is obliged to register each lien agreement and on or before October 1 of each year must prepare and forward to the minister of municipal affairs a return showing the names of all persons to whom advances have been made, and the amounts thereof. Fifth, provision is made in Saskatchewan legislation to give similar assistance to farmers in the local improvement districts which are administered by the minister of municipal affairs. Sixth, (a) the committee of the cabinet and the inspector for the district determine the amount of seed grain and supplies that a municipality may advance; that is, the cabinet in Regina decides the amount that each municipality can advance within the municipality. (b) Saskatchewan legislation provides that the municipality shall not advance in my year seed grain and supplies of a greater value than $200 in respect of any one quarter section, (c) On farms of 320 acres or less of cultivated land not more than sixty per cent of such acreage is to be sown.

Alberta has a slightly different arrangement, though the same in principle. In Alberta under the Seed Grain Loans Guarantee Act of 1938 the procedure is as follows. First, the Agricultural Relief Advances Act of Alberta provides that each municipality shall make provision to the satisfaction of the minister of municipal affairs for furnishing to necessitous farmers seed grain, fodder, feed grain, fuel oil and lubricating oil. A provincial order in council is passed authorizing the municipality to make a loan for such purpose. Then the municipality gives a demand note to the bank bearing interest at a rate not greater than four per cent for any such loans

so authorized, and the municipality takes from the recipient his promissory note bearing interest at the same rate. A lien is taken from the farmer by the municipality upon all crops grown in the year in which the advance is made and in the next ensuing three years. Provision is made in the Alberta legislation to grant similar assistance to necessitous farmers in municipal districts, by the minister of municipal affairs.
The amount of seed grain that may be supplied to any applicant, together with any seed grain which he is able to provide for himself, is set out as follows: If the applicant has arable land in condition for seeding amounting to 50 acres, he gets seed for 50 acres. If he has 100 acres he gets seed for 75 acres. If he has 200 acres he gets seed for 120 acres. If he has seed for 300 acres he gets seed for 165 acres, and of course that includes any seed he has of his own. If he has 400 acres he gets seed for 210 acres; if he has 500 acres he gets seed for 255 acres, and if he has 600 acres he gets seed for 300 acres. If the acreage of arable land in condition for seeding is other than an amount mentioned above, the acreage for which seed may be advanced is to be calculated upon the basis of the foregoing figures; provided further that no seed shall be supplied to any applicant in excess of the amount necessary for seeding 300 acres of land. Those are the provisions of the Alberta act, and they compare closely with those in the Saskatchewan act.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
Departmental administration, $425,720.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure that those of us who listened yesterday to the minister would wish to congratulate him upon the clear statement he made concerning the general matters under discussion. All of us who take part in this debate must realize that we are dealing with what is one of the most important questions and at the same time the most contentious problem before the country to-day. We cannot be insensible to the implications and the far-reaching nature of the questions under consideration at the moment. We

Supply-National Defence
should keep definitely in mind the fact that there is a strange unreality in ignoring the present unsettled state of the world. We cannot be blind to facts which are apparent, facts which tend to unsettle the minds of men as well as the stability of nations.
There is no hon. gentleman sitting in this chamber who does not thoroughly abhor war and all that it embodies and suggests. We have had an experience, still too fresh in mind, which indicates to us that victory is hollow and is a name applied to a state of affairs for lack of a better term. As the Prime Minister of Great Britain stated yesterday in the British House of Commons, in war there is no winner. No matter what one's personal feelings may be, there is nothing to be gained by burying our heads in the sands of whatever doctrine we wish to subscribe to; there is no use in burying our heads in the sands of north America and blinding ourselves to stark realities. We may detest the idea of armaments as such, and we may be loath to enter into any extended program to reestablish the defensive arms of Canada. It may shock our sensitivities and it may do violence to our sense of the fitness of things, but the fact remains that we are compelled in this chamber to face cold-blooded facts. In the words of Woodrow Wilson: "We are not here to argue what we want to do but what we may have to do."
No one could possibly accuse Great Britain of having been responsible for the rearmament race that is going on in Europe and the rest of the world at the present time. No one can possibly say that she, of all nations, has not lived up to the responsibilities that were hers as a member of the League of Nations. No one can possibly accuse her of having departed from her commitments until other nations forced her so to depart. Certainly no one can accuse us in Canada of having been irrational in the volume and extent of our expenditures on armaments. But, Mr. Chairman, we are compelled in 1938 to face the cold-blooded facts of the situation.
The matter under discussion on these estimates cuts cleanly across party lines, and in such remarks as I have to make I am speaking not in any political sense, but as a Canadian to my fellow Canadians. I shall address my remarks particularly to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Mackenzie) in the earnest hope that, coming, as they do, subsequently to his most able speech of yesterday, he will give them every consideration for what they may be worth.
51952-108J
First, may I quote his words as reported in Hansard at page 1650, and with his permission digest one of his paragraphs and make it more definite. He said:
When, sir, as we do now, we contemplate the broad principles of Canadian defence, and endeavour to define with some particularity the responsibilities that rest with governments, Canada must be prepared for the preservation of the best there is in these three nations-
That is Canada, Old France and Great Britain.
*-and the best there is within her own boundaries-the best there is in democracy itself-to take her stand, if need be, against brute force and might and ruthlessness, and, if need be, for high purposes to endure sore travail.
There is a statement which, taken by itself, means that the minister who made it at least has a sense of the needs of the situation. On the other hand, when we put into juxtaposition with that statement the estimates which are now before the committee, there seems to be a strange inconsistency. Let me put it bluntly to him:	Are we prepared
to defend Canada or are we not? If we are going to try to defend Canada with a defence that is adequate, the estimates before us for 1938-39 are sadly inadequate. If we plan to temporize with defence, perhaps these estimates are adequate. If we are not going to defend Canada at all, then clearly these estimates are vastly in excess of what they should be.
The hon. member for London (Mr. Betts) last night gave a most able presentation of his particular point of view in this matter, and I hesitate not at all to congratulate him sincerely upon his speech. He brought to the attention of the committee the necessity for us to defend particularly our harbours. The line of argument which he pursued was a telling argument. He suggested to us with great clarity that after all we were peculiarly vulnerable in such ports as Halifax, Saint John and Vancouver, and he insinuated though he did not directly state it, that these harbours could be attacked, and that we are at the moment absolutely defenceless and without protection for them and all that they represent. We know full well the vital necessity of those ports in time of war. We know full well how any Atlantic fleet would depend upon its ability to secure supplies, fuel and the like in such harbours as Halifax and Saint John, and how any Pacific fleet would lean heavily upon the harbour of Vancouver.
If we examine our own geographical position, we realize that an attack upon Canada could be made successfully only by air or by
Supply-National Defence

sea. We may, I think, safely assume that any attack by land from the country to the south of us is an absurd possibility even to contemplate, and accordingly the defence of Canada is at once confined to our harbours on the Atlantic coast in the east and to our harbours on the Pacific coast in the west; and the two coastlines. But no longer can we think of an attack as coming only from the sea. We must think of the air, and if we think of the air, then we find at once that the whole width of our boundaries should be defended. We have not 3,500 miles of border to defend with forts and batteries; but we do have our two coastlines as I have mentioned, and these two coastlines, it seems to me, can be defended at a relatively low cost.
I noticed from the minister's remarks as reported at page 1647 of Hansard that he gives us a word picture of our existing air defences. When one reads his statement, one is at once impressed with the fact that the locations of our training air fields have been well chosen, and if one did not know the actual facts as divorced from the picture he gave us, one would say that much has been done in Canada in the way of aerial defence. When we consider that we have training fields at Trenton, Vancouver, Esquimalt, Kamloops, Yarmouth, Sydney, Rockcliffe and other places, it would seem that the whole of the dominion has been fairly well covered with airfields. On the other hand, when one realizes the amount that has been spent on these airfields, the number of men with which they are staffed, the number of hours flown, and the number of persons who are being trained, one realizes how pitifully small is the Royal Canadian Air Force.
One does not criticize the air force for what they have done under the handicaps under which they have worked. One is, on the contrary, happy to think of what they have contributed so far, but naturally they have been grossly handicapped by lack of adequate equipment and by the small amount of money which they have had to spend. We must realize that all these things cost money and that naturally any government, which had to face such conditions as have existed and are existing in Canada, is loath to spend money on anything so contentious in Canada as armaments are, or as an air force is at the present time. On the other hand, we must realize the facts of the matter. When we realize that we have only a few aeroplanes- six, eight or ten at the most; I do not know what the exact number is-that will fly over 280 miles an hour; that we have absolutely

no bombers-I think I am correct in saying that-and that we are not prepared not only to defend an attack on our borders but also to repel the attacker by means of a counter attack, then we must realize that what we have done is hopelessly inadequate to meet the present situation.
May I correct a misapprehension? We have no aeroplanes of that speed at the present time, but eighteen are under order.

Well, then, we have yet
to fly 2S0 miles an hour in Canada; the situation is even worse than I thought. We have some training ships that are incapable of a speed of more than 110 miles an hour, ships which would merely clutter up the air in case of any complication, and which would certainly be useless in any active engagement. 1 do not think the minister heard a remark I made a moment ago. We have no bombers in our air force, have we?

Not yet
completed, no.

We are at the moment in
the process of purchasing ships for the Trans-Canada airways. They are certainly not wartime ships. Yet, if anyone goes to any country in Europe to-day he will find that all the passenger ships are bombers in fact as well as in name.
Convertible.

When one steps into one
of the Imperial Airways liners, he is not on board a passenger ship, he is on board a military plane which has been adapted for peacetime flying. WTe are about to embark upon a large expenditure for Trans-Canada airways.

Are not these
Lockheed-Electras fitted for bombing?

They are very small as
compared with the modern bomber. Their lifting load is very small and their speed very slow compared with the bombers flying on passenger air routes in Europe to-day; also, as the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) remarks, they are obsolete for that particular purpose.
It seems to me that we are challenged not only to build up an air force for the defence of this country but to build up that air force ourselves. The Canadian pilot has demonstrated that he is the finest in the world. That was said by the hon. member for Parry Sound (Mr. Slaght)

Supply-National Defence
last evening; it has been said over and over again in this chamber, and it is an established fact. We are the finest pilots in the world, and we should know more about flying than anyone else in the world. We should be able not only to fly ships but to build them as well. Only the other day I noticed that a factory is to be erected at, I believe, Malton-the hon. member for Peel (Mr. Graydon) is thumping his desk-for the manufacture of planes. Why cannot we in this country develop an aeroplane industry of our own? Why cannot we build those ships which we are to fly in our own air force? Why should we have to buy them outside? Why should we be in the position to-day that we go to the United States to purchase from them the ships for the Trans-Canada airways?
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver); In the defence services we are building practically all our own airships.

What is the capacity of
the plant?

It is
more or less in the experimental stage. I think six different firms are contracting.
All the engines are imported.
The engines are all imported, yes.
It is not a complete plant of itself?
No.
It is in part an assembly plant?
May I be allowed to give just a little information?
Order.
I am perfectly willing that the hon. member should do so, but he can make his speech later.
We have in Fort William an aeroplane factory which is at present employing 334 men, most of them experts.

I am glad to hear from the hon. member for Fort William that in that part of the world they are as air-minded as he says. On the other hand, with all due respect for what is being done at Fort William, I am speaking not of smaller efforts but of the large effort. If we are to have an air force in this dominion and to make the ships that we require, we shall not do so with 340 men in this factory or 120 men in a factory somewhere else. In other words, what plans, if any. has the government in mind
toward building our own ships in this dominion? What has the government in mind as regards the building of anti-aircraft guns? What has the government in mind toward either the purchase or building of the new pump gun? What has the government in mind toward the expansion of our ordnance facilities? We must realize, facing the facts as we are compelled to do, that in the event of war we must be able not only to put a fighting force into the air but to maintain it in the air. The whole question, then, is one not only of creation but of maintenance as well.
So I repeat that we must face the facts of the situation, a situation which we have had no part in creating. We are, if I may say so, innocent victims in a world of turmoil and strife, a world in which the existence not only of some nations of the world but of the empire itself is threatened, and of that empire we are definitely a part, and not only, let it be remembered, a traditional part but an economic part. Does any hon. member believe that our association within the empire is purely a traditional one? Where should we be were we a little country on our own in the northern half of the north American continent? What would happen to us in our present standing if we were to be attacked? We cannot be blind to the fact that the land-hungry nations of the world regard this dominion of ours as a juicy morsel on which to seize, and land-grabbing is not altogether unknown in these days. Japan has seized Manchuria, now Manchukuo; Italy has seized Ethiopia; Germany has seized Austria; Czechoslovakia hangs in the balance, and to-day Japan engages in another life and death struggle with China.
What is to happen next? Would any hon. member venture to rise in his place and say that there is to be no more of this; that this is the last; that we are through? Are we to be like the grasshopper in the fable who danced and sang, taking no thought of the winter to come; or are we to face, as I have said several times already, the facts of the situation? By no possible manner of means can we legitimately close our eyes to the situation which exists in Europe and which increases in seriousness, which hereafter may become less serious or may become more so. I think I understand the point of view of those living in various parts of the dominion who shun war and say that we should have no part in it because it does not concern us. But it does directly concern us if Victoria and Vancouver are laid in ruins, if Halifax and Saint John and even Quebec city are destroyed from both the sea and the air.
Supply-National Defence

The government, I fully admit, faces a difficult situation. But it seems to me that the minister in his estimates has endeavoured rather to save the face of the government than the body of the people. In other words, is this a policy of how little can we spend and get by, rather than how much do we have to spend in order to have security? I take second place to no man in deploring expenditure for defence; but when that expenditure has been definitely shown by the trend of the times to be necessary, perforce we must face the situation as it is and lay aside our individual feelings for the sake of the nation, looking at the broader panorama in its full width and implication.
Let us look for a moment to our sister dominion, Australia. We were told in the press of yesterday that $215,000,000 are to be spent in the next three years by a country whose British-bom population is not more than half our total population. Two hundred and fifteen million dollars will be spent in three years by one of our sister dominions. As the hon. member for London pointed out last night, Australia is spending for defence $4.30 per capita as against our 81.41.
Mr. MACKENZIE (Vancouver); We in Canada are up to $3.11 now.
As against Great Britain's
Yes.

We cannot maintain our
position as a nation and depend upon any sister nation, no matter how friendly that sister nation may be. We cannot possibly retain our status as a nation if we are going to lean upon one that is not part of us.
Why not?

The reason is perfectly
obvious. A mother will look aft"r her daughter without any expectation of reward, but cousins do not look after cousins on the same basis. That is the answer in a nutshell, as the hon. member for Essex East well knows.
No, I do not.

We cannot rely on the
fleet of another nation to defend us. Does the hon. member suppose for a solitary moment that the fleet of the nation to the south of us, no matter how friendly that nation may be, is going to rush up the Atlantic seaboard for the protection of Halifax? Does any hon. member think for a moment that its fleet on the Pacific is going to engage the fleet of Japan or some other nation that chose to attack Vancouver?
No question about it.

Do hon. members realize
the strength of the Japanese navy and to what that might lead as far as the United States is concerned?
How exceedingly anxious we were a short time ago to develop our status as a nation. As the minister pointed out yesterday, what he called "the Balfour formula" was acclaimed by many Canadians as establishing this dominion as a nation. Some of us have rejoiced in that fact; some of us have acclaimed from the housetops the fact that we are a nation. Are we then prepared to stand on our own feet or are we not? That is the question. Can we hope to preserve our entity as such and not be prepared to defend ourselves? There is no longer a north Atlantic fleet of the British navy. Let us not forget that fact, and let us not forget either that aeroplanes fly faster than ships plough the sea, and that a warring aeroplane is not like an aeroplane carrying passengers. A warring aeroplane does not have to get back; its job is to go to its appointed destination and drop its bombs; and after it has done its work, as one of the horrors of war, does it really matter whether it gets home? It sounds ghastly, but that policy was demonstrated over and over again by the enemy in the last war. Airships now fly the Atlantic one way, and it may not be long before the range of these ships will be such as to enable them to return to the field from which they took off or to an aeroplane carrier far at sea.
In the last war we did not experience hostilities within our own borders; in the next war there is no guarantee against that. Whereas there were some who said that the cry of the defence of one's home was a futile argument in 1914. that argument at least holds good to-day. The danger in which we live in this dominion is not the danger of being compelled to send an expeditionary force across the sea, but the danger of having our own homes destroyed by attack from the air. Let it not be considered as idle talk to-day to refer to the defence of our own homes, particularly the homes of those who live in our seaports. Air attacks are not unlike accidents; you do not know that you are going to have them until they happen. It was only a few years ago, as hon. members will recall that we looked up into the sky one day and saw some twenty planes, bearing the insignia of Italy upon them, flying through the air on their way to Chicago. True, that was a peaceful mission, but some of us wondered that day how long it would be before bombing planes of some enemy of the British commonwealth might be flying through Canadian air on other than a peaceful mission.

Supply-National Defence
I urge the minister, with all the earnestness of which I am capable, that in his estimates he give consideration not only to the point of view of how little we can spend to save our face but to the point of view of how much we must spend in order to save the body of this nation.
Will the hon. member indicate how much we should spend?

I am not a military expert any more than the hon. member for Selkirk, but I am discussing preparation in the face of the possibility of war. I am not here to state how much we should spend. The hon. member, however, knows quite well, living safely ensconced in the heart of the dominion, that he has nothing to be afraid of from the air. But how about those who live in Vancouver, Victoria, Halifax and Saint John? Their situation is entirely different. I can readily understand why the hon. member for Selkirk should have the point of view he has, but he does not face the situation which those who live on the seaboard must perforce face.
I implore the minister to look upon these estimates in the broadest possible way. In the light of his own statement of yesterday afternoon, with which he concluded his remarks, the possibility of war is not so remote that we can afford to ignore it and leave our policy to be decided after the guns have begun to thunder. We must face the possibility, as horrible and all as it is, that Great Britain may become engaged in another life and death struggle. We must try to visualize what it means to each one of us as Canadians, if Great Britain were to be defeated in such a struggle; yes, and to visualize as Canadians what would happen to us were we to be directly attacked. Every hon. member of this committee must face these decisions as an individual, and we have a right to require that our government should face them as a government.
Flights on the wings of oratory, arguments dressed up in all the detail of which every language is capable, and the subtlety of words, do not remove the fact that we are living in a wicked world wherein man is prepared to use force against his fellow man. All the sincere piety in the world is valueless when hostilities break out, and the arm of the invader is stronger than the arm of him who is merely pious. Again I urge the minister that, in the name of this dominion which we love; in the name of all the liberty and privileges that are ours as members of the British commonwealth; in the name, not merely of traditional loyalty or of effervescent
patriotism, but of common sense, we face facts fearlessly and plan our course, not under the urge that inspires military aggression but under our desire to be a nation, in fact as well as in name, ready and prepared to defend our shores and our homes against the ravages of a ruthless invader. Let us give thought, then, not to any hectic higgledy-piggledy expenditure of large sums for a navy, for an army and for an air force, but to adequate and reasoned protection against the only possible attack to which we are subject, namely, from the air or the sea, and let us have a permanent land force trained and equipped to meet any emergency which may arise.

I wish to express appreciation of the decision of the minister yesterday to precede his estimates with a statement as to general policy and to permit the discussion to cover a wide range. I feel that the statement he made yesterday will do much to allay unnecessary criticism and to give a better perspective of the intentions of the government. I am bound to say, however, that his statement does not answer all the questions, the anxious questions that are being asked by the Canadian people at this time. In this group we have withheld criticism until after the delivery of the minister's statement. We have given that statement some consideration. We appreciate the difficulties of the government in dealing with these questions. We are not unmindful of our responsibilities, and for that reason I do not intend to use any reckless language; for I fully appreciate the gravity of the situation confronting the Canadian nation at the present time.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) has reminded us not once but several times of our responsibilities. But I would point out that the responsibilities of the minister at this moment are even greater. He is aware of facts in regard to international affairs; he is aware of the decisions as to British government policy which have not yet been disclosed to the Canadian House of Commons. I would be the last one to suggest that he should take a meddlesome attitude toward international affairs, or toward British policy, but I think it most important that he should deal definitely with some doubts and uncertainties which are in the minds of the Canadian people. Let us be under no misapprehension. In spite1 of all that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey) has said the Canadian people most earnestly desire peace and they intend to work for peace.
Supply-National Defence

In my opinion it is the minister's responsibility to define more clearly Canadian policies, to give Canadian opinion courageous leadership and to provide a satisfactory basis upon which to unify Canadian opinion. May I suggest to him that this desirable result cannot be attained by any attempt to pacify the imperialists on the one hand or conciliate the isolationists on the other. As I view the question, unless some attempt is made to establish a plan of collective action by the great powers, there is little hope of averting a major world wrar in which Canada may be involved. We have been told by the Prime Minister that one of the most important guiding principles of policy at this time is the maintenance of Canadian unity. I submit that there can be very little unity; that he cannot satisfactorily answer the questions of anxious Canadian mothers at this time, unless he tells us more clearly how and under what circumstances or conditions Canada will employ the armed forces which he now asks this committee to provide. That is the important question, which I regret to say the minister did not adequately answer in his statement of yesterday.
If I criticize the defence policy outlined by the minister, it is not because I am opposed to defence as such. I regret very much that insinuations have been made from time to time misrepresenting my position or the position of anyone in this group in that respect, I say clearly I am not opposed to defence as such. The minister has strongly emphasized the idea that it is our duty to do something reasonable to protect our people and our country. I think he will not find any hon. member of this committee in disagreement with him on that score. What I have said and say now is prompted by a knowledge that defence involves much more than a haphazard expenditure of public funds on armaments.
He has not heard this group counsel inertia in the face of world trends of to-day. No one suggests that we should neglect our national interest and thereby to some extent court national extinction. I do not propose that we should leave our national defences in such a state of disrepair as to invite any lawless aggressor to come over and do with us what he pleases. I believe it to be the responsibility of any government to defend the country from external attack. I hope I make my position clear. We are quite as much concerned as the minister with regard to national security. We are quite as much concerned as the minister that our shores should not be ravaged or our homes laid waste. So I think we may eliminate from this discussion any insinuation that any of us
TMr. Massey.]
would remain supine should any attempt be made to ravage our homes or violate the territorial integrity of our country. But I submit that it is quite compatible with that desire for national security and national unity to question the purpose and the degree of armament proposed in these estimates.
These matters have been discussed in the British House of Commons. Only yesterday the broad lines of policy were laid down by the British Prime Minister. As was done in Westminster, so I submit broad lines of policy, may be laid down here, with more definite reference to the existing international situation and Canada's position with reference to that situation. These estimates mean that we are preparing to fight. True, . the minister emphasizes preparation for defence; nevertheless he did suggest the possibility of armed action in support of peace-time diplomacy, or of obligations to defend democracy. We should know now more clearly what the government's intentions are in this respect. The minister has not assured us that these estimates are solely for purposes of direct defence.

They
certainly are, every cent of them.

I have gathered otherwise from the statements of the minister as reported in Hansard. When he speaks of armed support of peace-time diplomacy and the defence of democracy, he is referring to external considerations. However, I hope that at a later time we may have his assurances in more definite terms. He cannot safely be indefinite in this respect.

subtopic: NIAGARA FALLS OBSERVATION BRIDGE COMPANY

speechtext:
The house in committee on Bill No. 15, to incorporate the Niagara Falls Observation Bridge Company-Mr. Damude-Mr. Sanderson in the chair.
On section 1.-Incorporation.
Mr. MaeNICOL: Mr. Chairman, as a member of the committee that considered this bill, I wish to say something about it before we * proceed any further. I must say that I enjoy very much speaking of that historic district

Niagara Falls Bridge
in which it is proposed to erect this bridge, and if there were more time I would enjoy it even more. The Niagara river frontier is one of the most historic districts in Canada, made famous first by those early French explorers whose bravery and ability to navigate the unknown wilds have never been surpassed. In the course of time it was found necessary to erect bridges over that great river. The first one to be erected, on the site occupied by the recent Falls View bridge that fell down, was erected in 1867. I do not know the date of the construction of the second bridge; but the third, the one that fell down on January 27 of this year, I believe was erected some forty years ago, in 1898.
As far as I can see, there is no reason for any hurry in considering this bill, in the first place because the state of New York has killed the bill as far as the United States side is concerned; and in the second place, to which I shall refer later, because of the proposed bridge above the falls that, I hope, will be erected some time later by Canada and the United States. While it is imperative that the cities of Niagara Falls, New York, and Niagara Falls, Ontario, should have at the earliest possible moment, a bridge erected at or about the site of the bridge which collapsed, we cannot hurry matters because, as I said a moment ago, the bill has been killed in the legislative assembly of the state of New York. So we are given ample time to consider thoroughly what is the best thing to do for that district.
There are several bridges left. First, there is the bridge below the escarpment at Queen-ston, called the suspension bridge. Second, there is the double-deck, steel arch bridge at the north end of Niagara Falls, the upper deck of which, I believe, is used by the Canadian National and perhaps other railways, while the lower deck is used by pedestrians and vehicles of one kind and another. Third, there is the cantilever bridge, perhaps better known as the Michigan Central bridge, immediately south of the lower steel arch bridge. Fourth, there is the Peace bridge itself, from the city of Buffalo across to Fort Erie on the Canadian side. So, if a bridge is not constructed on the site of the former bridge for another year, while the inconvenience may be great it is not a matter of extreme urgency.
The committee had before it two proposals, or rather one proposal and one objection. The objection was raised by the owners of the bridge that collapsed, the International Railway Company. They opposed the application of the Niagara Falls Observation Bridge Company, and it was interesting
indeed to listen to the proponents of the new bridge and to the statements of the representatives of the International Railway Company. Certainly their representations were not similar, and figures were presented to the committee that made me, for one, wonder on what we could base our judgment. The representatives of the International Railway Company gave figures as to the earnings of the bridge that collapsed, and as these were greatly at variance with the figures given by the proponents of the Niagara Falls observation bridge I believe we should have both sets of figures placed on Hansard. They stated-and their statement was not challenged-that those figures were audited by reputable auditors, and I do not believe any company, either the proponents or the opponents, would use any figures other than those which were audited. The figures submitted by the proponents of the Niagara Falls observation bridge were supposititious. I neglected to write them down, and there was no Hansard of the proceedings, but I did take the figures from one of the Niagara Falls newspapers, quoting what Mr. Suitor said in the New York state assembly. The figures quoted were higher than those submitted by the International Railway Company. As I remember, the income was estimated at between $500,000 and $600,000. On the one hand, we had an audited statement by the company and, on the other, we had figures submitted by the proponents of the bill at Albany, New York. It will be noted that the first action provided for in that bill is the issuing of $500,000 worth of bonds. Then section 12 provides for the issuing of securities not exceeding $7,000,000. In other words, the cost of the bridge was estimated as $7,500,000. Upon members of the committee questioning these figures and upon the proponents of the bill being told that the supporters of a similar bill before the New York state assembly had stated that the bridge would cost $3,000,000, the estimated cost was brought down to

$4,000,000. That figure was still considerably above the figure submitted by the International Railway Company as the cost of their bridge.
The International Railway Company were represented by one of the ablest engineers on the north American continent, Colonel Monsarrat of Montreal, whose reputation could not be added to by anything I might say in his favour. Colonel Monsarrat stated that he could build a bridge sufficiently large to take care of the traffic for between $1,125,000 and $1,500,000. Upon further questioning we finally got the Minister of Highways of Ontario to admit that $2,000,000 was to be used to purchase lands. Who knows how much the bridge will cost if the land has not been purchased already! If it was a private company the land could have been bought before anyone knew a bridge was to be built, but I am sure that this land will now cost a great deal.
The International Railway Company would not have to buy any land for their bridge, and they claim they can erect a new bridge and provide ample exit and approach. The people of Niagara Falls want a new bridge as quickly as possible, and the International Railway Company claim that they could have their proposed bridge in operation within a year. They claim also that they have a right to permission to build a new bridge. I do not want anyone to get the idea that I am against public ownership. I think my record in the early days of the organization of the Ontario Hydro-Electric Commission will stamp me as a public ownership supporter. But I am opposed to ownership that states a bridge will cost $7,500,000, and then reduces it to $4,000,000, when it is stated in the United States that the same bridge will cost only $3,000,000. We have too many bridges that cost far more than they are worth.
Figures were submitted to show that if this Niagara Falls observation bridge is built, even at a cost of $4,000,000, it will never be a free bridge. The proponents of the public ownership bridge say that their main purpose is to provide a toll-free bridge. Figures were submitted and were not disputed that the revenue from such a bridge would not be more than $325,000. Operating expense was put at $95,000, which leaves an operating income of $230,000. Allowing two per cent for depreciation, this leaves a net income of $150,000, and, less 5 per cent on investment, makes a deficit of $50,000. If a public ownership bridge is built, the city of Niagara Falls will derive no taxes from it. Many members of the Niagara Falls council have protested against the erection of such a bridge and against the expropriation of lands from which the city

already receives taxes. I should like someone to figure out for me how a bridge can be paid for when the net deficit is $50,000 per year. The figures submitted by the International Railway Company showed that it has been difficult for them to pay any dividend on a bridge that cost between $1,125,000 and $1,500,000.
The proponents of the bill stated that the bridge which was wrecked was not able to take care of the traffic. I was over the old bridge a great number of times, and while one might have had to wait a little while on a Saturday or a holiday, there was no difficulty whatever in crossing the river on weekdays. The old bridge had four traffic lanes, the number to be provided by the suggested bridge. If four traffic lanes were not sufficient on the old bridge, they certainly will not be sufficient on the new one. It was pointed out that the old bridge could permit handling
2.520	an hour in both directions. I assume it was vehicles that were meant, as we were talking about vehicular traffic, at the time. There would be no time when anything like
2.520	vehicles would cross in an hour. The evidence was that the peak was 900 an hour. Traffic figures were submitted which showed that the record day was the Sunday before Labour day in 1928, when 15.767 vehicles crossed the bridge. The second heaviest traffic day was the Sunday before Labour day in 1931, when 12,581 vehicles crossed. On the Saturday before the record Sunday in 1928 there were 4,323 vehicles, and on the Monday following, 6,653.
I shall take Colonel Monsarrat's word for it that the four-lane bridge did have ample capacity, and as the new bridge would have only four lanes its capacity would be no greater. It was clearly pointed out that if there were more customs officials and immigration officers stationed at each end of the bridge, then traffic would move much more rapidly; but on the other hand it was pointed out that neither the government of Canada nor the government of the United States would appoint more officers to have them standing at the end of the bridge twiddling their thumbs for nine days out of ten, or perhaps more than that, just so that they would be able to take care of the heavy traffic on the first and fourth of July, Labour day, Decoration day and some other holidays.
I went to the committee meetings with an open mind; in fact I have not yet stated whether I shall vote for or against the bridge; but what I did not like from the very commencement was the attitude of the promoters of the bridge before they appeared before the committee at all. What did the
